pros might not outweigh the cons. TLDR Summary: it probably isn't worth the hefty price tag. Cons:. -The price has doubled twice in three years. $21/month is what you'll have to pay to sync your notes on your phone, iPad, laptop and work desktop. If you can get by with three devices, you might be able to squeak by on the Starter plan. - One of the new "updates" by promoted by the developer is a new pricing plan. What a spin! You're telling me that one of the new "features" I have to pay for is a more expensive pricing structure? -Another new feature is the AI inclusion, meaning that machine learning will be used to read and sort your information. Only on the Enterprise plan is ownership of data guaranteed; check the privacy policy for how they determine ownership of what you upload. What you upload will be shared with OpenAi and other unnamed third parties, meaning that those audio files will share what your voice sounds like with an undisclosed third party. -In the phone app, you can export or download a note as a psf file. The only way to share is via a link or email. Pros:. -The Web Clipper browser extension. I've found it incredibly useful to be able to save pages and paragraphs from websites. -Scannable. The ability to convert image-to-text or image-to-pdf has been helpful, although it's a bummer the Scannable app costs extra. -Handwritting recognition? I don't use handwriting features often, but I like the idea of converting ink to digital format (replacing all of the Rocketbooks and smart notebooks I've tried with a regular old pen & paper). Neutral: Some features are a given with any note-taking app and I'm listing them here so it's clear why they don't help a consumer choose Evernote:. -Tags to sort your content. -Notebooks to organize by subject (Only 20 if you're using the Starter plan). -Templates. -Calendar integration (but tbh this is done better by the apps with strong email integration like Microsoft OneNote or Google imho)

Great App If You Know 1 Key Truth. FYI: I'm not getting paid for this review. Evernote literally changed my life from a business and networking platform - however - you've got to know one simple truth or Evernote just won't mean anything to you. The simple truth is: you cannot "dabble" with Evernote. Evernote was never meant to be just an app that you dabble and play with occasionally. If you use it like a general note application you'll never "get" all the hype about Evernote. The reason I know this is because that's what I never understood. I never understood why I heard so many business people raving about Evernote until I finally learned this: you have to jump in headfirst and put your ENTIRE LIFE into the application. When you do it will radically change everything. I categorize everything. Creative Ideas, expenses, projects, quotes, articles, my coaching notes for my son's football team, vacations info, trip planning, home remodeling projects, notes for business meetings, etc. And that's how EverNote is supposed to work. Think about putting all of your life into "notebooks" or storage bins. If you do that you quickly realize it's the app you seriously cannot live without.

Love the new features, and it's running much better. December 2025 I'm having trouble getting it to open linked notes that I haven't recently opened. I'm also frustrated with the Transcribe function, which sometimes works perfectly and sometimes simply invents things. I transcribed a couple of really clear photos of product packages a few days ago. One was transcribed faithfully word for word, bit the other was not. Evernote didn't transcribe anything that was written bit instead made up its own riff on the contents, like a high school sophomore writing a book report. It seems to me the transcribe feature has degraded, at least for phots. I really relied on it. —-xxx—-. August 2025 The program is running much more smoothly now. I still wish that headers functioned a bit differently, which I get into below. —- xxx —- I love the transcription feature. So far I've only tested this with pictures and screenshots (I think it also works with audio) and it's fantastic. I'm always capturing recipes, and I like to rewrite and work with them to suit me. Previously I would tediously type them out by hand, but now I no longer need to. —-xxx—- Regarding Headers: I only wish for a few improvements in these: - That you could use headers within tables, as I like the visual formatting of having most of the content of my notes within tables, and it would be nice to be able to create expandable / collapsible sections within these, as I don't always want to see everything at once. Collapsible sections would make for easier scrolling as well. ... - ... I wish notes did not "update" every time you expand or collapse a header section. These are not true updates, and it confuses me and wastes time when scrolling through recently updated notes to find something. It also causes problems when searching a note's history to look at changes and deletions, as it causes empty "updates" to appear when there have been no actual changes. .... Another time waster when I'm trying to find something. - It 's great that when searching inside a note the search function includes the content of any headers. What's not great is that searching expands any headers with content that matches, and then leaves these expanded, requiring me to manually collapse them, one by one. This is a real pain. Also, and again, this expansion causes the note to "update." ...-... I wish headers automatically collapsed when you navigate away from a note. I hate re-opening notes and having to collapse a bunch of lengthy headers before I can reach the note content. It would be cool if maybe they were like a menu whose contents appeared when your mouse hovers over the title, and whose contents you could click on, but which did not actually expand. ...-... That leads me into my final wish for headers, that they could be used like on website pages where, for say all the notes in a notebook, or perhaps all of a group of notes you selected, headers would automatically populate from a main / control page, and any changes you made to that main page's headers would push through to all the other notes in that group. Regarding other things I brought up in my original review, I still have not figured out the table of contents thing, and I'm still looking for an easier way to search on iOs. —- ORIGINAL REVIEW—- There is still nothing near as good as Evernote to replace it with. I thought about doing so repeatedly during recent years, but there's nothing that combines the functionality of web clipping, notebooks, tags, links to other notes, PDF attachments/annotations/searching, etc. all with pretty much instant updating across multiple devices. I use it nearly much every minute of the day, far more than any other software or application. I store everything in it except for passwords and other highly sensitive information. Writers, speakers, comedians, and musicians, whose careers may depend upon flash-bulb types of ideas, may find Evernote indispensable. Install Evernote onto several devices and they stay in sync automatically via the "cloud.". Find notes by browsing notebooks or TAGs. Sort them to isolate the ones with sound recordings. Search by keyword (which can be in note titles, notebook names, TAGs, or text), and find them that way. Evernote can even find handwritten words in pictures. And if you knew you recorded a great note but cannot remember the first thing about it, search for it by location, since Evernote can geotag every note you make. I use Evernote for all kinds of things. As a drummer, I often cannot transcribe rhythm ideas before they escape my imagination. Location and time of day may help me remember how I felt just then and restore any of the, well, MEANING behind the idea. Evernote's use of the iPhone's camera in 2025 feels like stepping back into the smartphone Stone Age — except even those early cameras at least attempted to focus. 1. Evernote Leadership Refuses to Incorporate the Most Basic Usability Features by Refusing to Fully Use the iPhone Camera APIs. It doesn't matter whether you're capturing a document, a receipt, a page of notes, or an object: Evernote's camera regularly delivers blurry, unusable images. And it's not because the device lacks capability. I'm using one of the most advanced cameras Apple has ever shipped — and yet Evernote somehow manages to turn a high-end sensor into a blurry mess. Why? Because Evernote's camera:. - Offers zero focusing capability. - Offers no manual controls of any kind. - Offers no ability to switch lenses. - Ignores iOS's native camera APIs. - And constantly misfires its "auto scan" routine. Even the most trivial iOS apps — scanning apps built by one person in a weekend — manage to focus correctly. However, that's not a priority for Evernote. Instead, they prioritize other things for development-things that pale in comparison to addressing the unbelievable shortcomings of Evernote's use of the camera. 2. Evernote's Failures to Effectively use the iPhone Camera Hinders Users Instead of Helping Them. Evernote loves to tout how their camera is designed for "fast capture.". Let's be clear: nothing about Evernote's use of the camera is fast. And nothing about it is useful. Instead of a clean workflow, the user is forced into:. - Retaking scans multiple times. - Moving the phone back and forth in the hope of achieving some kind of "Kentucky windage" focus manually. - Backing up farther than necessary, leaving the subject too small in the picture. - Wasting time in some work around using the iPhone camera app outside of Evernote, thereby cluttering the user's photo album, and requiring the user to cull through photos imported to Evernote to delete them or just live with receipts and pictures of documents amongst family photos. - And worst of all: wasting time on a task that should take two seconds on any other app. This isn't a minor annoyance; it's a core function that Evernote has failed at for years, despite much earlier versions having the ability to focus the iPhone camera. 3. Evernote's Blatant Disregard for the User. The most galling part? Evernote has received widespread feedback on this issue — repeatedly — and continues to ignore it. Users have complained across:. - App Store reviews. - Evernote forums. - Reddit. - Social media. - Support tickets. And yet Evernote remains silent. No transparency. No roadmap. No acknowledgment. No fix. Meanwhile, competitors (including free apps!) offer:. - Superior autofocus. - Better scanning pipelines. - Cleaner UI. - Higher-quality images. - And actual support and responsiveness when something falls short in their app. Evernote, on the other hand, seems perfectly comfortable pretending their broken camera is "good enough.". It isn't. 4. A Productivity App That Fails at Productivity. This is not a cosmetic issue. It's not a "nice to have.". A note-taking app that sells itself on capturing information must — at minimum — be able to focus the camera and capture a readable image. Evernote completly fails at these, and that demonstrates a fundamental failure of design, engineering, and customer care. In sum, Evernote's use of the iPhone camera is an incredibly weak link that undercuts the entire app. If Evernote wants to call itself a modern productivity platform, it needs to fix the basics before pushing new features. User for more than 10 years... My life is run on Evernote. More than 15 years now. I started with the free version and only upgraded with paid version a few years ago (needed more monthly storage). I share my enthusiasm for Evernote with everybody, even though I've yet to actually utilize or optimize all of its features. I run my life and small business on it. It's a great product! If I could change anything...I REALLY wish there was still a FREE VERSION to use with my clients — especially my disabled and advanced seniors, who are less tech saavy and live on very tight fixed incomes. (they have some version of a smart phone, but not computers.). If there was a FREE VERSION — with for smaller usage customers, I could recommend it all day every day. But a seven day trial is not enough to learn the benefits of Evernote if you're new to such a platform or under duress of a medical condition or life crisis. It's such a product existed, I (a long timely user and paying customer) could more effectively assist family, friends, and clients in time of need. I could login and quickly set them up for organized productivity to reduce their stress (and mine) if I could CREATE SHAREABLE pre and post private medical appointment NOTES and PLUS personalized reminders, LISTS for tasks, shopping, meal prep, and KEEP updated prescription and symptom RECORDS. Especially with the dictation and transcribe capability. As many of them have physical challenges. Not just limited tech experience. A special product offering for that population would be a boon to an aging, retiring, and unwell population in the U.S. and BETTER ENABLE them stay organized, maintain autonomy, get the most out of the time they have... When things take longer, and they tire more easily. Or become frustrated by complexity of life and aging or adulthood. I truly love Evernote's simplicity... and it's many advanced features. It's ideal for students, retirees, and seniors. Especially the infirmed and overwhelmed with their own independent living and medical challenges. Unfortunately, there no longer seems to be a FREE version for me to recommended to those I teach and assist in "the business of living". I have long recommended Evernote and share my great enthusiasm for the EASE and USEFULNESS of the product. It's just not affordable. A free (or almost) product that could be used by individuals I've described would be a boon for all of your paid customers as well. In my own personal experience, once you've used Evernote for free... You'll never use anything else. Eventually becoming a paying customer when circumstances improve or change. Like in my case ... I couldn't see myself using anything else and I just needed more storage. For me, Evernote would be the ideal product for everyone of all ages, if there was a very small one time annual fee for those on limited and fixed incomes. Who are just starting off in life or struggling financially. Personally, I think we should be teaching elementary students to use Evernote! Imagine a world where everyone was much more productive, less overwhelmed by the complexities of 21st-century living, and felt a little more in control of their own personal worlds. 💪

Infuriating update! I've been using this note-taking app for quite some time now. While it has always lacked a few creative features—like a lasso tool to flip objects horizontally or vertically and other tools that are common in similar apps—I still chose to stick with it because of its simplicity and the freedom it gave me when writing, drawing, or organizing my files. However, this new update, although maybe well intentioned, has taken away a lot of that freedom and has made the app frustrating to use. For example, when I draw a straight line and hold it to keep it clean, it randomly transforms into an infinity symbol or some other unwanted shape. When I draw a triangle and want to erase part of a line or remove the fill inside, that's no longer possible without constantly going into shape settings and adjusting options every single time I want a different triangle. This becomes a hassle, especially because I work with math every day—drawing graphs, sketching diagrams, and writing equations—so I need quick and precise control, not extra steps. Also, another infuriating issue I've run into is when I try to draw a simple diagonal line while holding to make it straight snd clean. For some reason, the app automatically bends the line into a 90-degree angle instead of leaving it diagonal like I intended. If there is a way to turn off this "auto-correction," it is extremely difficult to find. I've searched through the settings with no luck, and it shouldn't be this hard to disable something so basic. Simply selecting a line to make it longer is becomes infuriating. On top of all this, I can't even switch back to the previous version of the app, which is really disappointing because I preferred how it worked before. To give credit where it's due, I still really like the file system—it's easy to save, organize, and import files, which I appreciate. But I honestly wish I could return to the previous version or at least turn off these forced shape edits. Some new features would be nice, sure—but not at the cost of usability. I feel I have less freedom than I did before. As if I'm forced to take notes or draw a certain way and not how I prefer.

Honestly kind of trash. I really wanted to like Goodnotes, but the app feels unnecessarily complex and frustrating to use compared with other note-taking apps. Basic functions are buried behind menus and settings that are not intuitive, and the learning curve for simple things like scrolling, selecting text, highlighting, and syncing is way higher than it should be. The cloud syncing has also been disappointing. I imported a very small PDF on my computer and it sat with a spinning cloud for several minutes, while the same note appeared on my iPad with completely blank pages. For an app that is supposed to work seamlessly across Apple devices, syncing should not feel this unreliable or slow. The highlighting experience is another major frustration. If I want a clean text-based highlight with proper square borders around the words, I have to hold down on the text with my finger and manually select it. I cannot simply use the Apple Pencil to select the printed text in the same way. Using the Apple Pencil highlighter instead just creates a drawn stroke, which does not give the same clean, precise borders around the actual text. For an app designed around iPad and Apple Pencil note-taking, having to constantly switch between the Pencil and my finger for basic text selection feels poorly thought out. There are definitely a lot of features in Goodnotes, but that is also part of the problem. The app feels overcomplicated rather than intuitive. Simple tasks require too many steps, syncing feels inconsistent, and the Apple Pencil experience is more limited than I expected. I switched because I wanted a better note-taking experience, but so far Goodnotes has made basic tasks feel more difficult than they need to be. A note-taking app should make studying faster and easier, not make users spend time figuring out how to perform basic functions.

Don't waste your money - Bait-and-switch: Essentials Won't sync between iOS and Android. The entire reason I purchased GoodNotes is to do sync across all the devices in my ecosystem. Unfortunately, the reasonably priced "Essentials" tier at $12/year locks you to sync only within the IOS Ecosystem, and won't cross-sync to Android devices. Annoyingly, it won't sync web content across those two ecosystems either. If you sign in with an ID used on ios, it will HIDE web content created on PC or Android. They had to go do active development specifically to BREAK sync to force you into a higher-cost plan. You have to upgrade to the $36/year "Pro" plan to allow cross-device sync. This is a terrible bait-and-switch - when I first tried GoodNotes, they claimed a "paid subscription" would be required to enable cross-device sync. "Essentials" is paid, but won't do the job. Nobody should be wasting their money on this app as a trial: expect further erosion of capabilities, now that they've figured out how to game their user base into paying more for a feature that should be a baseline capability. When Onyx, OneNote, and Notion can do this at their free tiers, there's no reason to use GoodNotes. In addition, the sync logic is buggy, causes data loss, and isn't workable with an intermittent internet connection. Undocumented bug: GoodNotes requires a full-time, full-bandwidth connection to the internet _at all times_: it's a wrapper around the web service, with no ability to edit/update/display/store a local replica for note taking when you're in an area with marginal internet, and no cellular coverage (like many lecture halls and engineering spaces, the places that I NEED to take notes in). I you open a notebook with marginal internet, it'll just spin for minutes until it downloads a fresh copy of your cloud save, and will then be subject to random freezes and stalls as the app attempts to sync the entire thing regularly. Recording continuously under these conditions is also impossible, so don't think you can record the lecture, then listen later and update your notes - nope, the recording is corrupted and intermittent, too. Don't waste your money evaluating it: you'll be disappointed. Would give negative stars if I could.

UPDATE: The developer response to this says they "respect [my] right to make choices about [my] data," but they did not express any plans to allow users to make choices about their data. After this first impression left a bad taste in my mouth, I was disappointed to see more aspects of the app appear pretty cavalier about gathering extraneous user data with no option to decline. Analyzing user metrics can be helpful, machine learning and LLMs can be helpful; and they will still be helpful when their datasets are sourced with consent.

That was a fantastic experience and I routinely used the app for marking up pdfs, signing things, and regular bullet journaling. I recently updated to an M4 iPad Pro/Pencil Pro and this new version of Goodnotes and I'm honestly frustrated. The pen performance is not as good. I write quickly and the pen engine (or whatever is translating my input) in this new version routinely leaves small tails on my letters and inputs that I did not intend unless I stop the pen fully before pulling off the screen. From doing some research it appears this has something to do with the prediction built in to the software? I've tried everything I can find: "reduce latency" is on, stroke stabilization low or off, different palm rejection settings, etc. Nothing changes the underlying problem which is that the app requires you to write more slowly than I do in order to have neat endings without phantom strokes being put on the page. This is disappointing and I have ended up using the Apple Notes app for more things now as a result. If anything can be done on this, fast writers like me would greatly appreciate it. The rest of the app is fine. AI note taking didn't work that well for me, but I never used it for that sort of thing. I didn't even really want to buy the new app, but got tired of the nagging prompts and decided to "upgrade" with my new iPad. I wish I hadn't.

Below average for PDF markups. I had a consistently frustrating experience using the app for PDF markup. Handwriting input was especially difficult to use well. It was inaccurate in ways that created constant friction rather than speeding anything up. A clear example was the app repeatedly converting a capital "I" into the number "1." Errors like that were surprisingly hard to correct cleanly without giving up and switching to the keyboard, which disrupted the whole workflow. Instead of feeling like a smooth handwriting-first experience, it often felt like I was fighting the recognition and cleanup process just to produce basic, readable notes. Separately, the comment tool does not export reliably. Even when using typed comments and selecting the correct export settings, including flattened PDF with comments enabled, the comments fail to appear in standard PDF viewers. This makes the feature unsuitable for sharing or submitting annotated documents. Overall, the app does not provide a dependable workflow for creating and exporting annotated PDFs, particularly when the output must be viewed outside the app.

One fatal flaw destroys accessibility. It's great to have it sync with family and Google Home. But my primary use case is shared lists, and Keep has horrible accessibility. On iOS, there is a three second timeout after which keyboard focus leaves a list item, finalizing the list item with whatever text was input. If you are a slow typer or use alternate input means - or even if you just need a few seconds to form your thoughts - google keep interrupts you. You end up with empty list items because you didn't type fast enough. You end up making multiple list items instead of one. You end up cut off with half written list items. Unless you are a fast typer who always has fully formed thoughts ready to input without pause, this app is nearly unusable. This no doubt demonstrates the limitations of a formulaic user testing process. I have a hunch that the Keep QA team has list entry items ready to go, and quickly runs through tests, rather than testing real world use cases - especially with a variety of accessibility considerations.

App Crashes On iOS devices. I've been a long-time user of Microsoft To Do across different platforms, and while it works flawlessly on Android and Windows, the iOS version has become nearly unusable due to a major issue. After launching the app on my iPhone, it crashes within 1–2 minutes, abruptly closing and returning me to the main menu/home screen. Worse, this crash seems to cause temporary instability in the overall iOS system — other apps freeze or hang briefly, and the device becomes sluggish for a few seconds after the crash. This goes beyond a minor bug and feels like it's affecting the core performance of iOS itself. In contrast, the app performs smoothly on Android and Windows, syncing tasks as expected and delivering the productivity support I rely on. The cross-platform experience would be great if not for the iOS-specific issues. I hope Microsoft addresses this bug soon, as it significantly impacts usability for iPhone users and undermines trust in an otherwise reliable productivity tool.

Simply The Best. I've found that the best apps are those that appear simple on the surface and become more advanced when you need other features. It will do everything Notes or Bear or any other notetaking app can do on the surface. It's minimalist and beautiful. Not cluttered by insane UI like Evernote. But you can also create advanced bases and templates that allow automatic categorization and interlinking of notes so you can always find old notes again. It's built on a fundamental idea that your notes are just a collection of markdown text files in a folder. So the app is incredibly fast, future proof, and light weight. No custom files, and no bloat. Like others have mentioned, there are community plugins that are fantastic. Anything you can do in Evernote and Notion, you can do in Obsidian but way way better. Took the tip from the dev to make sure "Keep Downloaded" was on in the Files app... it had always been set this way on Mac but found that it wasn't on iPad... so now that it is, now it's wait and see... +1 star for developer responsiveness... star #5 is pending resolution of the crashing issue... ...still the occasional crash from restart — general iCloud instability is probably causing this — as well as file updates that get "stuck" syncing between Apple devices sharing iCloud — need to take Apple to task on this since the sense I'm getting is iCloud is not resilient or robust enough to justify the huge 2TB storage solutions that Apple is selling. Since I can see signs aside from Obsidian that point to iCloud as the culprit I will award the 5th star to Obsidian because I will not penalize it for what is evidently an Apple issue.

Lost Many Stories. I heard many good things about this app for story planning and writing, so I decided to give it a try so I can properly organize my markdown files and write stories. Only had it for a day and never have I been more horrified. The last thing I expected was for Obsidian to completely make my markdown files disappear from my external drive for all my fanfiction works. Thankfully my original fiction remained untouched. That would have been worse if it did. All the worldbuilding, notes, research, and chapters I wrote for those fanfics are gone. Like they never existed. Did the usual troubleshooting, but nothing brought it back. I was lucky I was able to file recover in one of my cloud drives to get the files I have lost. I'm terrified of losing my works and don't want a repeat of this experience, so I'm moving over to a different app. It's a huge deal breaker if my works are lost this easily with Obsidian. Not only that, I'm not able to access my external drive on the app, which is another huge deal breaker as cross platform is a must have and I don't want to be paying a subscription just to be able to cloud sync + cross platform for all my creative writing works when I can simply just one time purchase external storage then plug in then write. I have no plans of using Obsidian again. Don't recommend for serious writing. Only if you're working on one device and are using cloud sync, that is. If you want to write seriously and/or rather use an external storage for creative writing, I suggest finding a different app. Overall, hugely disappointed since I heard so much good things about this app for notetaking, planning, and creative writing. So, I had expectations. Unfortunate that Obsidian didn't meet them. Edit: I decided to give it a chance again, but this time through Obsidian Sync. It was a bit unintuitive to figure out how to set it up, but figured it out eventually. However, as much as Obsidian is great on computer, the app had so much delay when it comes to writing on mobile. Which is unfortunate because cross platform is a must for me and compared to other apps and softwares I have used in the past like iA Writer, Scrivener, LibreOffice, Ulysses, Bear, etc., the delay when you press onto a new line then try to type since it's trying to sync is noticeable. The plugins also act funky on mobile. Ended up refunding it the same day I got Obsidian Sync and just sticking with the current app I use to write. Because of the delay issues, plugins acting funky, and the fact that Obsidian does mess with my files, I'm still keeping it at my current rating. Obsidian is only good on computer and if you choose work locally only without cross platforming and syncing. As much as I did enjoy what Obsidian offers, it just isn't optimized well enough and I don't really trust that it'll prevent my drafts, research, notes, and ideas + concepts from disappearing like it never existed or corrupting, randomly duplicating files or folders, and reliably syncing to the cloud. Otherwise, I still highly recommend looking at a different app if you need that cross platform, no typing delay, and apps that have some built-in features that plugins from Obsidian offers. Like I said, if you only work locally, not cross-platform, and not cloud sync, Obsidian is great on computer.

Love it. As a writer, I have tried a wide range of writing apps—from the built-in iPhone Notes and Pages with its bare-bones functionality to more specialized tools like Scrivener. But as of 2026, I can say with confidence that Obsidian is better than all the others. Yes, it is very geeky. Yes, the developers tend to overthink the application, which makes Obsidian feel overloaded in places. But—and this is important—none of that is mandatory. You can use Obsidian as a simple note-taking app that gives you plenty of freedom to organize your workspace and workflows to suit your needs, and only later, gradually, explore its more advanced features if and when you want to. In short, whatever tasks you may need a note-taking app for, Obsidian is definitely worth trying.

An extensible, flexible tool for power users. Obsidian is a highly flexible app that gives users many affordances with regard to customizing both the appearance and behavior of the app through its extensive list of community plugins and themes. With over 2,000 plugins, you can do almost anything you want with Obsidian—task management, writing, brainstorming, research, etc. The app itself is also local-first and used Markdown, meaning your notes are stored on your device where Obsidian and third parties can't snoop on your notes. Markdown is a plaintext format that is commonly used in everything from messaging apps, documentation sites, blog posts, and more. Because your notes are in a common, plaintext format stored on your device, you'll be able to access and edit them even if Obsidian disappears. Obsidian itself is developed by a small team of just seven engineers as of January 2026, and they don't rely on VC funding at all. They update the app frequently—my favorite changes as of late have been Bases, the latest mobile app design overhauls, and widgets for mobile. (Psst, if an Obsidian developer is reading this, support for push notifications on mobile would be a godsend for any task management workflows since it'll enable reminders that work without me having to use an external app like TaskForge.). Now for as much as I praise Obsidian, there are aspects about it that will put some people off. First and foremost, syncing your notes across your devices will require you to pay for a subscription service. Furthermore, the extensibility of the app has made it daunting for new users, as the app (by default) does not come with many of the features that users have come to expect from using other note-taking apps; Obsidian can be tailored to most workflows, but that takes a lot of trial and error to reach. Essentially, if you're someone who doesn't mind needing to customize your app to get it working, Obsidian provides plenty of features and affordances for you. Beyond that, there are other note-taking apps out there that might suit your needs better, like Joplin, Bear, or Notesnook.

Tried to lean on the native support resources, but the presentation and vocabulary require either a foundation of understanding, or a companion resource to understand the guide. There's got to be a way to configure this program in a "simple mode" that intuitively unfolds further functionality as needed rather than exposing the entire spread of tools expecting new users to know enough to pare back those features that may not be necessary early on (backlinks!?!). Additionally, many of the plugins are clearly written by coders and developers for other coders and developers to understand. Additionally I'm not a programmer much of the learning curve can become cumbersome and fosters a sense of futility. Good example; what's the virtue in obsidian creating daily notes for dates where no notes were created? The slash command is handy, however I often don't know the difference between similar concepts such as bookmarks vs links vs backlinks etc, and furthermore what practical purpose these seemingly different features enable. Just my two cents but if anyone has a killer way to learn this tool I'm all ears. If you are on the fence, I say try it out, hopefully it makes more logical sense to you!

More than just a note-taking app. Obsidian is a great note-taking app. Using markdown, it's easy to write and format notes, link between them, and port them between platforms and even open them in other apps. With Obsidian, there is no concern about your notes being lost when the developer sunsets their app, raises the price, or sells out to a Microsoft. But where Obsidian really shines is its extensible architecture and large library of plugins. It's easy to add features, adjust how Obsidian looks, and integrate with other apps. This makes it possible to set up Obsidian as a the core of your daily organizing routine. Both a personal nerve center and a second brain. It's not perfect. It opens a little more slowly than simpler note-taking apps, especially when loaded up with a bunch of plugins. It may occasionally crash (in particular, some community-made plugins are not very stable). Syncing between devices can be a little finicky if you don't use Obsidian's native sync service. Overall, though, Obsidian is amazing and has won a place on my "must-have" app list.

Poor implementation of access to photos. iOS gives developers better options than what OneNote appears to be using here. An app can present Apple's private photo picker, where you can choose any photo at that moment without granting the app permanent access to your whole library. Many apps do exactly that. With Limited Access, an app can also provide a "Select More Photos" / "Manage Photos" button that invokes iOS's permission screen from inside the app. OneNote apparently isn't giving you that convenient path—or isn't handling the modern picker correctly. So the awkward workflow you're seeing is not an unavoidable iPhone limitation. It's largely a OneNote behavior/design issue. One workaround worth trying is:. Photos → select photo → Share → OneNote. That hands the specific photo to OneNote directly and normally shouldn't require OneNote to have general access to the photo library. Otherwise, Full Access is unfortunately the least irritating solution if you frequently insert photos into OneNote.

Mac Support. OneNote is phenomenal on my phone and Windows desktop. I use it all the time. The problem is I also have a Mac laptop. OneNote used to work on the Mac, but now is unusable on the Mac because it does not reliably save changes. This means I will type to-do items on the Mac, trust they are stored in my system, and then they are not present on my phone and windows computer. I instead have to use the online version in a browser window on my Mac. While inconvenient, this would be acceptable if the online version were good. However, the online version is missing multiple functionalities, namely the ability to sort tabs alphabetically. I have been using OneNote for years and have hundreds of tabs. Not having them alphabetical is a significant time suck as I am trying to quickly reference important information in a meeting, but cannot find it. I have been working with OneNote so long and so much of my information and GTD system is there that I will continue to use it for now. However, due to their refusal or failure to keep their web and Mac apps up to speed with their Windows apps, I would not recommend OneNote to new users, especially if you anticipate any possibility of having an Apple device someday. I also would not recommend new users start OneNote because if they dropped the functionality of a once useful application (Mac), I do not know what else they will someday decide to drop the functionality on. For example, if the app on my phone stops working, I'll need to drop OneNote altogether and start the laborious process of transferring all my systems into a new platform. Summary: great on certain devices, not on others.

Occurs on new and existing notebooks. Persists after app reinstall and multiple device restarts. Fingers only (no Apple Pencil used). Workarounds:. Two-finger drag selection works. Mobile Must Step It Up To Be Crowned King. First off, 5-stars to OneNote Desktop. Unfortunately, to take the note application throne, users MUST have seamless synch and relatively equivalent capability across desktop AND mobile. As of 6/26/2025, this iOS app doesn't sufficiently hit that target. I realize that mobile is not Microsoft's wheelhouse and I suspect Apple is not making improvement easier. The reality is that OneNote iOS usability has barely improved in the last 3-5 years. That said, the starting capabilities of OneNote's features compared to everyone else in the game (Apple, EverNote, Google, Notion, etc.) are unrivaled: desktop UX, backup/revision history {pivotal!!}, Office integration, page linking, format customization, in-app search, files/images, etc. Synch has slowly gotten much better, which is massive, but its mobile UX is so severely lacking that I am considering another switch at this point (after migrating from Apple to OneNote). This app still feels like operating a desktop website on mobile and it's crippling for workflow. I have core pages that suffer fatal typing lag, viewing/organizing notebooks is often impossible, major features/options from desktop are inaccessible, cross-platform translatability to/from any Google/Apple products is a massive chore, they removed the native 'Look Up' function, synching issues are still commonplace (but remedied with superior backup/history options). At the end of the day, I need my mobile note interface to be as useable as desktop or the entire system crumbles. Apple Notes is far, far superior on mobile but absolute garbage on desktop and backup/Cloud utilization. We use our phones much more than our CPU and because of its size/power constraints, the mobile UX/UI bar MUST be proportionately higher to meet user needs. The first company to master both sides of the coin will definitively own the kingdom. I look forward to amending this review if this app does improve.

Fantastic except for one confusing problem... More user friendly than Todoist- also looks better because of recent updates. I think it is the best to do list all that exists. Full stop. And I've tried way too many. The only problem it has: I use the date property in my tasks to mark their deadlines, if they have deadlines- when they've got to be done by. I usually try to complete those tasks long before the deadline comes. How should I use the calendar feature in TickTick to schedule my tasks with time blocking? If I put them on my calendar for when I will do them, then the date property no longer represents the deadline for the task. So, I simply can't use the calendar for time blocking. Isn't that supposed to be the main purpose of having a calendar inside TickTick? Unfortunate. Adding a separate date property called "deadline" would be awesome. For most people, only a small portion of their tasks would have true deadlines. The current date property could be used to indicate when the user plans to complete the task. The new "deadline" property would represent when they need to complete it by, at the latest. To be able to filter tasks to see only ones with deadlines would be great. To sort by deadline would be great too. Then you could reschedule your tasks in the calendar using the primary date property while still being able to keep track of their deadlines. Users could also view both when they plan to complete the task as well as when the task is due on the calendar. Those two dates would need to be visually differentiated of course, so users could tell them apart. Some casual users might never understand the purpose of the extra "deadline" property, and that's totally fine. If this was done, TickTick would be a near perfect app.

this app is one of the best things in my life and i literally evangelize it to anyone and everyone. i've been using tick tick for a few years now. important background info: i LOVE planning, i love categorizing, i love organization, i love note keeping and collecting and compiling information and media of all kinds. i love being able to customize and design any system i interact with to my needs and preferences as much possible. (i am an engineer and also autistic so when i say i love this stuff, i mean it. it's a genuine passion and hobby for me). ticktick is fantastic for so many reasons, the fact that it's cross platform is already just a huge huge plus. but i think ticktick's design philosophy is what makes it so great. there are so SO many features, there are so many way to customize things, there are so many ways to tailor your tick tick exactly to your needs. if you want simplicity, you don't have to deal with using extra complex features that you don't need, especially since oftentimes complex or intricate functions and options are actually a hindrance for those who don't need it. with tick tick, you can make your lists, notes, whatever, as simple as you want. you don't need to deal with unnecessary complications if you don't want them. nor do you have to deal with the visual clutter of features you don't even use. this is a common issue i find on program and app design, where the excessive amount of options and buttons and features make them difficult to navigate and ultimately i will stop using them. and i love that tick tick puts so much work and effort into providing a wealth of options for customization ad well as options to interlink various notes, tags, media, you name it. but they also understand that is not what everyone needs, and they make it so so accessible and easy to just make simple lists without extra hassle or having some useless premium feature shoved in your face every time you open the app. for someone like me, i use basically all of the functions and features, i have created a wiki of sorts for various notes, i even use the link feature to link to notes in my native notes app! i love that you can create note folders/lists. its perfect for me as I can keep EVERYTHING i need in one place. i have a list that's just full of resources and user guides for my electronics/tools and other things i reference a lot. it's so amszingly helpful. I have a note list that contains helpful keyboard shortcut cheat sheets for various apps, and tick ticks sticky note feature allows me to pin those to the screen when i need them! i have a note list for shopping and wishlists, projects i want to do in the future. i even have a list of notes ABOUT tick tick (because i am not normal about this obviously lol) including an in progress visual user guide im working on for my friends because i want to convert them, a note of various features i think would be great additions, user feedback, a list of things to add to my tick tick. i could give so many more examples of the amazing ways you can use this app to make it perfect for what you need, but i genuinely doubt anyone is still reading this far haha. as i said at the bringing of this novel of a review, lists and organizing and planning is a hobby and passion to me. if i get to spend a weekend entirely making and arrange lists, information, and spend time and energy to do it efficiently, affectively, accessibly, with optimized and streamlined design and of course above all, approachable, usable, easy to understand, and something that i can actually keep up with. balancing simplicity and readability with my love for automation, detailed descriptions and breakdowns of tasks, as well as notes and information i find relevant. i will be on cloud nine having the time of my life and then show off my work to my lowed ones who are very patient with me haha. so you can TRUST ME when I say this is an AMAZING app, i love it, and i know what im talking about ;p it's the best one ive used a

Exceptional Work! Honestly, TickTick stands shoulder to shoulder with the best productivity apps out there. It handles continuity, syncing, and day to day task management extremely well. As a core to-do list manager, it really shines. But no app nails every single category, and TickTick has a couple spots where it could level up. The Pomodoro feature is the main one. It doesn't really need its own bottom tab just to show a single "Start" button. That space could be used for something more functional. The timer would make more sense sitting inside the "Home" tab, right next to your tasks, so it naturally supports the list you're actually working on. A Pomodoro should feel integrated, not separate. The Habit Tracker could also benefit from duration tracking. If I plan to read for 15 minutes but end up reading for 25 minutes, that extra effort should be reflected. And yes, there's the Pomodoro timer, but it doesn't fully connect to either habits or tasks, so the ecosystem never quite syncs together the way you'd hope. And clearing out bad habits could definitely be more intuitive and front and center. All that said, TickTick is still an excellent app. For what it offers, it provides exceptional value, and the overall experience is hard to beat. With a few thoughtful adjustments, it could easily become the gold standard for productivity apps.

The import from a spreadsheet is perfect for my grad classes to easily copy and paste from the syllabus and import the tasks into Todoist. The different ways to view the task lists are flexible depending on my needs for that list. I love that I can set something to remind me every few days to do something and with the additional paid for features, I can keep on top of everything even more granularly. It is the perfect tool and I have not come across anything I've wanted to do that it cannot do. Their help section on their website is fantastic for figuring out how to do various things, no matter what I dream up. I used the free version for a while, which worked great, but about 6 months in, I realized the paid for version was worth it for the additional projects and for the deadline so I could have various school projects show up daily before the deadline and I could still remember when it HAD to be turned in. It would be immensely helpful to be able to filter our shared project view by "assigned to me OR no one" but you simply can't do this! Argh! Beats travel-specific apps for travel planning. I was planning a 10-day motorcycle trip and tried so many different apps to organize everything and use as a hub for hotel info, sight-seeing locations, time management, maps, file attachments for tickets and national park maps, etc...but every app was a major flop. A quick monthly sub to unlock the map view made Trello the nearly perfect tool I was looking for. The only thing missing was auto-calculating time between map locations, but I was able to manually do it and use a few customized and color-coded tags to put that info on each card to see at a glance. Everything else was perfect: being able to use my board offline in remote areas, being able to share the board with my husband so he had access to all the info, attachments, map layout, adding dates to harness the schedule view, adding comments to track ideas, hyperlinks to web content and navigation routes, notes for check-in info at hotels and timed park entry, even being able to check off the things we got to see and what we didn't have time for. Trello did all of this SO MUCH BETTER than tailor-made travel apps like Wanderlog. Trello is just so versatile. Obviously great for trip planning, but also project tracking for freelance work, and creative hobbies like sewing projects. One of the best apps out there.

Great... If You Enjoy Being Locked Out of Your Own Business. To be honest, Trello used to be a great productivity tool — until Atlassian showed up with their magic trick: locking paying users out of their accounts with surprise 2FA prompts nobody ever set up. Brilliant. Imagine running a business, managing projects, staying on top of deliverables... and then suddenly you can't log in on desktop because Trello decided you should have 2FA credentials that you never received. No recovery codes. No setup flow. No warning. Just *poof* — productivity gone. The cherry on top? You can't even contact support because you need to log in to do that — which you obviously can't, because, well, 2FA. I'm two days behind on major work, stuck on a mobile app UI that feels like it was designed as an afterthought, and completely locked out of critical project boards on desktop. This isn't a bug — this is a UX disaster dressed as a "security feature." And while Trello's parent company Atlassian might think they're tightening security, they're really just tightening the noose around their own product's credibility. For a platform built on the promise of helping businesses stay organized, this rollout was anything but. If you're running a serious business, look elsewhere — until Trello figures out how to secure accounts *without* locking out their users in the process.

THE BEST TOOL FOR ANY PROJECT! I have been using Trello for years, and people in different organizations are amazed by the level of efficiency you can achieve with it. I have introduced Trello to various companies and NGOs, and I highly recommend it. Of course, you need to learn how to integrate Trello into your workflow, but it definitely helps! I usually don't write reviews, but today I felt it was time to share my thoughts! And God bless the developers, because the free version is incredibly useful and helps people at many levels, from students to dreamers, keep everything organized! I would like to suggest an enhancement for the "due date" feature. While the cards are currently organized by due date, it would be extremely beneficial if they could also sort by specific times. When multiple cards share the same due date but have different times, it can lead to confusion. Having the ability to view and organize these cards by both date and time would greatly improve clarity and efficiency. I've also noticed that recently, when I open the app on my phone, the cards do not appear in the same lists as they do on my computer. Ensuring that the lists are synchronized across devices would greatly enhance the user experience. Thanks for looking into this Trello Team! However 5 starts for the app!
